title: Rinzai and Soto
hookLine: Rinzai stresses koans and breakthrough; Soto stresses just sitting; each honors the other
carry: a koan or just sitting: two doors, one house

lines: ONE GOT A QUESTION WITH NO ANSWER.
cards: Two people come home from a weekend at a Zen center. One says her teacher gave her a question with no logical answer, and she pressed on it every sitting until something cracked open.
The other says his teacher gave him no question at all. Just sit, the teacher said. Don't wait for anything; the sitting itself is it.
They compare notes and wonder if they went to the same religion. They did. They just walked into two different schools of Japanese Zen.

teach.b: First, Rinzai. It takes its name from the Chinese Chan master Linji, known in Japan as Rinzai.
It stresses the koan, a short story or question from the old masters, like the sound of one hand, that can't be solved by thinking it through.
A student works with a koan in sitting and in private meetings with the teacher, hoping for a breakthrough called kensho, seeing one's own nature. Second, Soto.

It traces itself through the Chinese Caodong line and, in Japan, to the teacher Dogen. Its central practice is shikantaza, roughly nothing but sitting, or just sitting. Dogen taught that practice and awakening aren't two.
You don't sit to get enlightened later; the sitting, done fully, already expresses it. Third, each has the other's tools. Rinzai students spend long hours in zazen, sitting meditation.
Dogen himself wrote about koans, and Soto teachers use them. Some teachers call the difference one of emphasis, where each school leans, more than a wall between them. Fourth, two doors, one house.
Some people are drawn to a question held until it gives way; some to sitting with no goal at all.
Both call their way Zen, and both point at the ox, you might say, from the pictures just finished.
Teachers in some lineages train in both.

how: Rinzai Zen students sit zazen and work on koans in private interviews with a teacher; Soto Zen students practice shikantaza, just sitting, often facing a wall. Both schools hold retreats, chant and do work practice, and some centers draw on both.

o: Rinzai and Soto, two Zen emphases in one sitting tradition
the Chinese and the Japanese versions of one school
two rival Zen sects that reject each other's practice

s: Dogen himself wrote about koans, and Soto teachers use them.
Rinzai takes its name from the Chinese master Linji
Rinzai is the Japanese reading of his name.
the two schools share no practices
Rinzai students sit zazen, and Soto teachers also use koans; the difference is emphasis.

games.q: you ask a Soto teacher how long you should sit before you get enlightened. what is the teacher most likely to say, following Dogen?
o: sit until a koan breaks open.
the sitting itself, done fully, is already it.
awakening comes only after years of study.
games.why: Dogen taught that practice and awakening aren't two. Soto stresses just sitting, with no goal held out ahead.

practice: For the first half of the sit, hold one simple question lightly, without answering it: who is breathing? For the second half, let the question go and just sit, with nothing to find.
At the end, name one thing each half offered you, without picking a winner.

wordCard.voice: Two schools. Rinzai, stressing the koan and sudden breakthrough; Soto, stressing just sitting, where practice is already awakening. Two emphases, one sitting tradition. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese (shikantaza): 'nothing but sitting' or 'just sitting', the central practice of Soto Zen.

carryVoice: Your line: a koan or just sitting: two doors, one house. Rinzai and Soto, and no winner to pick. Until tomorrow.
